Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: At just 21, Ethan had already stepped into the role of public defender, a job that demanded sharp focus and unwavering confidence. Yet, beneath his professional exterior, he carried a heavy burden from his past. Ethan was a refugee, having fled a war-torn country where uncertainty and danger loomed at every corner. The memories of that chaotic time remained etched in his mind, often surfacing in jarring and vivid images. He found himself haunted by flashes of violence, the sound of gunfire reverberating through his thoughts as if it were happening all over again. Each time he felt that familiar sense of threat, the memories would rush back, pulling him into the chaos of his past, as if the danger of those moments was still alive within him. Each time these memories surfaced, they triggered a sense of threat; ordinary sounds, like the rustle of papers in his office or the hum of the air conditioner, would make him jump as if under attack. Once the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical - not something that had happened, but something that was still happening, leaving him in a state of heightened alert. Once the memory had surfaced, he couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present - the traumatic events felt as though they had simply moved into his body rather than dissipated, amplifying his anxiety. Once the memories of violence broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical, as if the chaos and danger he had escaped were still very much alive within him, waiting to strike again. Ethan began to believe that the world was an inherently dangerous place, leading him to constantly scan his environment for anything that could signal trouble. This conviction only deepened his reliance on maladaptive strategies, as he felt compelled to check the locks multiple times and avoid any situations that could expose him to danger, reinforcing his belief that he was powerless without these measures. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof he had that his life had changed beyond repair, reinforcing his negative view of himself and his belief that he was fragile. Each time the flashback came, it deepened his conviction that he was fragile and that he could not trust his own mind, leading him to think that if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with him. This belief that he was permanently changed kept dragging him back to the moment of trauma, as if he needed to continuously locate where he had been lost, making the memories surge with renewed intensity. This belief drove him to employ maladaptive strategies, as he felt that avoiding situations and checking locks were necessary measures to cope with the perceived danger, reinforcing his view that he was powerless without them. This perception of constant danger drove him to employ maladaptive strategies, such as checking the locks on his doors multiple times and avoiding crowded places, as he felt these were necessary to maintain some sense of safety in a threatening world. If he had concluded that the world was dangerous and he was defenseless, staying home and employing these strategies was not avoidance - it was the only rational thing to do. In the quiet of his apartment, unusual silence became his enemy. When he was alone, he felt a thick tension in the air, as though something catastrophic was imminent. This hypervigilance had become a part of his daily existence; he would frequently check the locks on his doors, convinced that something or someone was lurking just outside. The constant need to protect himself reinforced his belief that the world was inherently dangerous, leading him to conclude that his safety was always at risk. Coupled with this constant readiness for danger was an overwhelming sense of emotional turmoil. Even when he was not actively recalling the traumatic memories, he would experience the intense feelings associated with them, leaving him in a state of anxiety without any clear trigger. This emotional chaos made it difficult for him to articulate his experiences, leading him to avoid conversations about his past. He feared that discussing the event would only reveal how fragile his mind truly felt, as if he was teetering on the brink of losing his sanity. Ethan's thoughts were often consumed by the need to monitor himself closely. He had come to believe that these strategies were necessary for survival, yet with each act of avoidance, he silently confirmed his fears that he could not manage the world without them. He would scrutinize his own mind for evidence of unraveling, certain that showing any sign of distress would confirm the dangerous world he had come to believe in. Each time he resorted to these safety behaviors, he felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that he couldn't manage without them, confirming in a wordless way that he was indeed more fragile than others. This reliance on safety behaviors only reinforced his negative self-appraisal, as he began to internalize the idea that needing these precautions meant he was weaker than others, trapped in a cycle of belief that he could never truly recover. Each time he resorted to these safety behaviors, he reinforced the negative belief that he could not manage the world without them, deepening his conviction of fragility. Whenever he found himself in a social setting, he would deliberately steer conversations away from the topic of trauma, worried that others might inadvertently remind him of the harrowing experiences he had fled. This avoidance extended to interactions with colleagues, as he withdrew from conversations that might lead to discussions of hardship or suffering. He rationalized that by keeping his thoughts and experiences to himself, he could maintain a semblance of control over his life and stave off the emotional pain that threatened to consume him. However, the memories persisted, becoming increasingly intrusive. Ethan would often feel as though his body was reliving the traumatic moments, as if he were physically transported back to that time of crisis. This reliving of the trauma heightened his sense of threat, leaving him on edge even in safe environments, and pushing him further into his avoidance behaviors as a means of coping. When the threat felt this close, these checks weren't mere compulsions; they were the only way he could find some semblance of safety in a world that felt overwhelmingly perilous. This bodily reenactment was terrifying; it reinforced his belief that danger was always lurking, ready to strike when he least expected it. Each flash of memory intensified his hypervigilance, creating a self-perpetuating cycle where his negative appraisals of the world fed into his maladaptive strategies for coping. He felt trapped in a relentless loop of fear and avoidance, convinced that stepping outside of his carefully constructed defenses would expose him to unbearable vulnerability. As the weeks turned into months, Ethan became increasingly isolated. This withdrawal only deepened his conviction that he was fragile and that the world was beyond his control, affirming his negative view of himself and reinforcing his belief that he would never truly be safe. His relationship with his partner began to suffer under the weight of his silence, as he withdrew emotionally, unable to share the burdens he carried. Every time his partner reached out, he felt an urge to retreat, fearing that any discussion of his past would reveal how deeply affected he was by his experiences. It was an exhausting cycle; he wanted to connect, but the fear of exposure kept him locked away in his own mind. Finally, after months of struggling, Ethan decided he could no longer endure his internal turmoil alone. He recognized that the strategies he had employed to protect himself were only deepening his distress. The need for help loomed large in his mind, but so did the fear of what it might reveal about him. What frightened him most was the prospect of confronting the very memories he had tried so hard to avoid. Yet, a small glimmer of hope remained; perhaps, through seeking help, he could learn to navigate the dangerous world he believed he lived in and reclaim a sense of safety and connection with those he loved.
